synopsis: A frozen video encoder supports jointly learned inverse dynamics and latent-conditioned future prediction. On natural videos, constrained continuous actions capture richer changes than the tested quantization scheme. A separately supervised controller makes this space usable for short-horizon planning, but latent predictability, visual quality and planning accuracy are different objectives.

problem.text: Natural videos provide abundant action-free observations but no shared embodiment. An inverse dynamics model can explain a transition by encoding motion, environmental noise, or even the future image. The problem is to constrain that information while retaining complex changes such as a person entering a scene, then connect the learned space to interpretable control.

contributions.text: The regularization study compares sparsity, VAE-like noise and vector quantization under a common prediction setup. Continuous variants span a broader capacity range; the tested discrete approach remains close to prediction without action conditioning.

Scene-cut and cycle-consistency diagnostics test copying and transfer separately. Qualitative transfer suggests spatially localized, camera-relative actions, including movement transferred from a human to a ball.

A controller maps labeled actions and visual context into the pretrained latent space. Planning results demonstrate a useful interface, with label-free world-model pretraining but action-labeled downstream controller training.

inputs: Natural video frames for pretraining; consecutive encoded states for inverse dynamics.
At planning time: current and goal images plus candidate real action sequences.
outputs: Latent actions and predicted future visual representations; optional decoded frames.
Real action sequences selected by external CEM optimization.

steps.name: Encode and infer transitions
steps.detail: Frozen, frame-causal V-JEPA 2-L produces states. The inverse dynamics model observes consecutive states, including the future, and infers a default 128-dimensional latent action. The ViT-L world model uses past representations and frame-wise AdaLN-zero action conditioning to predict the next representation.

steps.name: Restrict the information channel
steps.detail: Sparse actions combine an L1 constraint with norm and variance/covariance/mean terms against degeneracy. Noisy actions use a Gaussian-prior formulation; discrete actions use a codebook with unused-code resets. These alternatives constrain information, without guaranteeing that it describes only controllable causes.

steps.name: Learn the real-action interface
steps.detail: The later controller minimizes L2 error against inferred latent targets. Two self-attention blocks process the previous frame representation, followed by cross-attention with actions embedded by a three-layer MLP. A linear projection produces the latent action. Frame duplication compensates for tokenization that groups two frames per latent.

training.text: World model and IDM train jointly with teacher forcing on YoutubeTemporal-1B: 16-frame clips at 4 fps, 30,000 iterations, batch 1,024. Muon uses learning rate 0.02 and AdamW 6.25×10⁻⁴, with 10% warmup, cosine decay and weight decay 0.04. Appendix A reports approximately 12 hours on 64 H100 GPUs.

The visualization decoder is a separate causal ViT-L trained with L1 and perceptual losses. Controllers train on DROID or RECON for 3,000 iterations, batch 256, using eight-frame clips duplicated to sixteen and AdamW learning rate 10⁻³.

inference.text: IDM-conditioned rollouts require observed future frames and serve as an idealized diagnostic. For planning, the controller replaces that unavailable inference path: candidate real actions and recursively predicted states generate latent actions and future states. CEM minimizes distance to the encoded goal.

DROID uses horizon 3, 300 candidates, 10 elites and 15 CEM iterations. RECON uses horizon 8 at 4 fps, 120 candidates and one iteration, restricting trajectories to a straight-line action divided over the horizon. These are different protocols.

equations.explanation: Appendix A's training objective: s denotes encoded visual states, pψ the world model, gφ inverse dynamics, zt the latent action and Lz its regularization. The future state is both a prediction target and an IDM input.
Appendix A, Equations (1)–(2): C scores candidate real actions a over horizon H; sg is the encoded goal, ŝ a predicted state, and c the controller. Predicted states feed subsequent predictions.
Equation (3) compares cumulative planned and ground-truth translations. This endpoint displacement error, reported in meters, differs from the latent-space cost used to optimize a plan.

results.setting: DROID-trained controller; recorded Franka Panda validation trajectories; 64 sampled episodes from 16 videos, four frames at 4 fps, horizon 3.
results.comparison: Noisy/mid 0.11; sparse/high 0.13; discrete/high 0.14; V-JEPA 2-AC 0.15; V-JEPA 2 + WM 0.05.
results.interpretation: Table S1 places the best noisy model ahead of V-JEPA 2-AC but behind the specialized comparator. The measured quantity compares planned and recorded displacement; it is not a closed-loop manipulation success rate. No uncertainty is supplied.

results.setting: RECON-trained controller, unseen-video goal-image evaluation; horizon 8 at 4 fps, straight-line planning with one CEM iteration.
results.metric: RPE and ATE, lower is better
results.interpretation: Table S2 supports improvement over NoMaD, not parity with NWM. The supplied protocol does not state a navigation evaluation count or uncertainty; the table does not label metric units.

results.setting: Kinetics videos with artificially exchanged endings; IDM receives the transition including the new future.
results.metric: LPIPS without / with scene change, lower is better
results.interpretation: Large error increases argue against perfect next-frame copying in this test. They do not establish zero leakage or causal disentanglement; Figure 6 shows some future content entering the prediction.

results.setting: Infer on video A, apply on B, re-infer and apply back on A; two-second predictions on Kinetics and RECON.
results.metric: Original / transferred LPIPS, lower is better
results.interpretation: High capacity retains better absolute reconstruction after transfer. Random-video transfer has no uniquely defined semantic target, so cycle consistency is evidence of reusable transformations rather than a semantic action accuracy measure.

results.setting: Separate Appendix D sweep mixing DROID and YoutubeTemporal-1B before controller training.
results.value: Noisy model: 0.14 at 0% DROID, 0.09 at 10%, and 0.06 at 75% or 90%.
results.interpretation: The benefit depends on regularization and data mixture. These sweep configurations are not interchangeable with Table S1. Table S3 also contains an unresolved controller-LPIPS anomaly.

limitations.text: Static regularization cannot adapt to each video's action complexity. Frozen representations may hinder prediction. Direct planning in the latent space remains open; Appendix B's qualitative sampling analysis shows mismatch between inferred and sampled high-capacity continuous latents.

Rollout quality does not reliably rank planners. Scaling improves IDM prediction, but longer training produces the clearest planning improvement; more pretraining data has no consistent planning trend in the reported sweep.

Controllers can fail when the robot arm begins outside the image. Without visual representations, the displayed action-only controller leaves the arm static. These examples limit claims of a universal action interface.

Reporting ambiguities remain: the noisy regularizer has a printed negative KL sign despite prior-matching prose and an additive training loss; Figure 11 and Table S2 disagree on RECON rollout values; Table S3 prints 0.9 for noisy/100%-DROID controller LPIPS. No corrections are inferred.

reproduction.text: Reproduction requires the frozen encoder, natural-video data, predictor/IDM, decoder for LPIPS, and labeled DROID/RECON controllers. Preserve frame duplication and each planner's budget. Appendix A supplies optimizer settings and regularization sweeps, but not a complete IDM architecture, explicit Low/Mid/High-to-coefficient mapping for every table, or full evaluation seeds and split identifiers.

Proposed checks: compare capacity settings with identical controller data and planning budgets; separately compare visual-context and action-only controllers across camera viewpoints. Measure latent prediction, decoded error and displacement error independently, including uncertainty across seeds. These are reader proposals, not completed experiments.

reasoning.text: The foundational-work classification and latent-action-pretraining/world-simulator subcategories fit this study. The catalog's Not applicable quadrant is treated as a scope choice. Architecturally, a frozen encoder, separate IDM and forward predictor, and later controller are distinct components. Joint training does not establish one backbone jointly predicting future states and executable actions. Inverse dynamics learns the latent interface; controller-conditioned prediction supports inference-time planning.

discussionQuestions: How much of cycle consistency reflects camera-local motion rather than reusable semantic actions?
Which capacity should be chosen when the best rollout model differs from the best planner?
Would viewpoint-balanced controller training preserve control when the arm starts outside the frame?

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title block and arXiv margin
evidence.detail: Title: Learning Latent Action World Models In The Wild. Authors: Quentin Garrido, Tushar Nagarajan, Basile Terver, Nicolas Ballas, Yann LeCun, Michael Rabbat. Affiliations: FAIR at Meta; Inria; NYU. Margin identifies arXiv:2601.05230v2 [cs.AI], 20 Jan 2026.

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, Abstract and Introduction; p. 4, Section 3
evidence.detail: Natural video lacks action annotations and a common embodiment; inverse dynamics must separate useful transition information from exogenous noise and future-state copying.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and caption; p. 5, Section 4
evidence.detail: Figure 2 routes frozen encoded observations to inverse dynamics and a latent-conditioned forward model. Section 4 identifies frozen V-JEPA 2-L, joint IDM/predictor training and frame-wise AdaLN-zero.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 3, Sparsity / Noise addition / Discretization
evidence.detail: Sparse constraints include norm and VCM terms; the noisy formulation matches a standard Gaussian; quantization uses codebook resets. The methods regulate latent information.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Section 4; p. 17, Appendix A, Latent action training
evidence.detail: Default ViT-L predictor, 128-dimensional actions, teacher forcing, YoutubeTemporal-1B clips, optimizer schedule and full regularized loss are specified. Appendix A reports 12 hours on 64 H100 GPUs and coefficient/codebook sweeps.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 4, decoder paragraph; p. 17, Appendix A, Decoder training
evidence.detail: A separate ViT-L decoder uses causal attention and L1 plus perceptual losses to visualize predictions and compute perceptual metrics.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Figure 4 and Section 5
evidence.detail: IDM rollouts use future frames. Prediction error serves as an operational capacity measure; sparse and noisy sweeps span wider ranges than the tested discrete codebooks.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 5a, Future leakage, Figure 6 and footnote 3; p. 8, Table 1
evidence.detail: Scene cuts test whether a latent can copy the next frame. Table 1 high-capacity rows report sparse 0.20→0.50, noisy 0.21→0.54, discrete 0.29→0.68 LPIPS. Figure 6 retains some future information but reconstructs poorly.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, Figure 5b and transfer protocol; p. 8, Figure 7, Table 2 and discussion
evidence.detail: Cycle consistency re-infers transferred actions and measures two-second LPIPS back on the source video. Table 2 reports original and transfer columns for Kinetics and RECON. Figure 7 demonstrates human-to-ball motion transfer and return.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 8, caption and Section 6 conclusion
evidence.detail: Only the person near the source motion's position is animated in the two-person example, motivating the camera-relative, spatial-locality interpretation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Section 7 Controller training and Figure 9; pp. 17–18, Appendix A Controller training
evidence.detail: The controller uses L2 latent targets, previous-frame representations and real actions. Appendix A details two self-attention blocks, cross-attention, a three-layer action MLP, projection, frame duplication and training settings.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Section 7 Planning performance; p. 18, Appendix A DROID protocol, Equations (1)–(3)
evidence.detail: Franka Panda recorded-video evaluation uses 64 episodes sampled from 16 validation videos, horizon 3 and four frames at 4 fps. CEM uses 300 candidates, 10 elites and 15 iterations; reported displacement compares cumulative planned and dataset translations.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Appendix A, Planning protocol for RECON
evidence.detail: RECON uses 120 candidates, one CEM iteration, straight-line trajectories, horizon 8 and 4 fps. Evaluation uses ATE and RPE, with further details referred to NWM.

evidence.location: PDF p. 20, Appendix C, Table S1, both panels
evidence.detail: Noisy Low/Mid/High controller errors are 0.13/0.11/0.12 and planning errors 0.49/0.11/0.10 m. Sparse/high is 0.13 m, discrete/high 0.14 m, V-JEPA 2-AC 0.15 m and V-JEPA 2 + WM 0.05 m. No uncertainty columns are present.

evidence.location: PDF p. 20, Appendix C, Table S2, planning panel
evidence.detail: Noisy/high reports ATE 1.40 and RPE 0.40; NoMaD 1.93 and 0.52; NWM 1.13 and 0.35. No uncertainty or unit labels are supplied in this table.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 9–10, Section 7 rollout/planning discussion; p. 11, Figure 11
evidence.detail: Controller LPIPS and planning error are plotted against in-the-wild prediction error for each regularizer. Intermediate capacity improves visual prediction, but planning minima need not coincide with rollout minima.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Figure 12; p. 12, Section 8
evidence.detail: Model size, training duration and data quantity affect IDM prediction. Planning benefits most clearly from longer training; model-size effects differ by regularizer and data quantity shows no significant planning trend.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Section 9; p. 19, Appendix B and Figure S1; p. 20, Appendix B closing sentence
evidence.detail: Authors identify static constraints, frozen representations and direct latent planning as limitations. Sampling uses codebooks, Gaussian priors or SGLD, with qualitative UMAP mismatch for less-constrained continuous latents.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Appendix D, Table S3, planning rows and discussion
evidence.detail: DROID mixture weights are 0, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90 and 100%. Noisy planning error changes from 0.14 at 0% to 0.09 at 10% and 0.06 at 75%/90%; sparse changes from 0.14 to 0.13 at 10%.

evidence.location: PDF p. 34, Appendix H; p. 36, Figure S12; p. 37, Figure S13
evidence.detail: Qualitative examples show failure to generate an initially invisible arm and static predictions when the controller has no visual-state representation.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Noise addition equation and prose; p. 17, Appendix A full loss
evidence.detail: The noise equation visibly prints a negative beta times KL divergence, while prose describes prior matching and Appendix A adds latent regularization to prediction error. The supplied paper does not resolve this optimization-sign ambiguity.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Figure 11 lower-left and upper-right panels; p. 20, Tables S1–S2
evidence.detail: The RECON Controller LPIPS panel spans roughly 0.38–0.48, while Table S2 controller values span 0.21–0.26. Figure 11's V-JEPA 2-AC line also lies below the 0.15 reported in Table S1. Exact results here follow the identified tables, without reconciling the displays.

evidence.location: PDF p. 21, Table S3, Noisy / Controller LPIPS / 100% DROID column
evidence.detail: The printed entry is 0.9, despite adjacent values near 0.10 and prose about improved rollouts. This apparent anomaly is preserved without guessing a correction.
